images.caption: A small dam, which is mostly just the gates, controls the flow of water from Lake Whatcom into Whatcom Creek.  This basically keeps everyone happy.  Lake Whatcom doesn't get too low, in the dryer summer months so people who live around the lake can still use their boat docks and water intake pipes.  In the winter, extra water is let down the creek so the lake doesn't get too high.  Back in the 1980s, regulating the lake worked okay, but when too much extra water was sent down the creek, it flooded businesses along Iowa Street.  It was a classic case of the diverging interests of citizens in different areas.  Since then, better dikes have been built along the creek and the greenway area serves as a harmless place to put the water.  Hurray for greenways and trails.

images.filename: Whatcom Creek using it's flood relief feature (40270673262).jpg
images.caption: I thought it would be neat to ride the Whatcom Creek Trail to see the raging creek, but soon found myself in the creek. Sign said "water over trail," but I proceeded. Soon, tho, water was raging up towards my knees. I turned back. Then I went home to get my camera and approach the water again from both sides of the flooded area using Fraser Street, rather than the trail, to get through. I think the floodplain greenbelt is working as planned. Trail should be okay when water recedes. That's what a floodplain is for.

images.filename: Waterfall in creek near Lake Whatcom, July 12, 1895 (WAITE 49).jpeg
images.caption:
Notes in inventory: New Whatcom, Wash. Waterfall in creek about 4 or 5 miles from Lake Whatcom .This may be Tinling Falls .An early town on Bellingham Bay formed by the merger of Whatcom and Sehome in 1891, assisted by the coming of a large number of settlers from Kansas was named New Whatcom. This town later combined with Fairhaven to form the city of Bellingham. Whatcom is an Indian word meaning "noisy rumbling water" referring to Whatcom Falls.   PH Coll 291.164
